claim: Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen known for causing hospital-acquired infections.
source: Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen known for causing hospital-acquired infections.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the medical literature about A. baumannii's role in healthcare settings.

claim: The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified A. baumannii as a critically high-priority pathogen in dire need of new therapeutic strategies.
source: The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified it as a critically high-priority pathogen in dire need of new therapeutic strategies (Tacconelli et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tacconelli et al., 2018.

claim: A. baumannii is a member of the 'ESKAPE bugs'.
source: Consistent with its classification, A. baumannii is a member of the 'ESKAPE bugs', a term referring to six pathogenic species (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter spp.) notorious for causing hospital-acquired infections and their ability to escape antibiotic treatments (Rice, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rice, 2008.

claim: A. baumannii can gain new functions, including antibiotic resistance, through horizontal gene transfer via plasmid conjugation.
source: A. baumannii can gain new functions, including antibiotic resistance, through horizontal gene transfer, notably via plasmid conjugation (Di Venanzio et al., 2019; Hamidian et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Di Venanzio et al., 2019 and Hamidian et al., 2014.

claim: A. baumannii can gain new functions, including antibiotic resistance, through natural competence for transformation.
source: A. baumannii can gain new functions, including antibiotic resistance, through horizontal gene transfer, notably via plasmid conjugation (Di Venanzio et al., 2019; Hamidian et al., 2014) and natural competence for transformation (Godeux et al., 2018; Godeux et al., 2022; Harding et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2010; Vesel and Blokesch, 2021; Wilharm et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Godeux et al., 2018; Godeux et al., 2022; Harding et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2010; Vesel and Blokesch, 2021; Wilharm et al., 2013.

claim: A. baumannii can withstand desiccation, disinfectants, and survive on surfaces for extended periods.
source: Beyond its resistance to antibiotics, the bacterium can withstand desiccation, disinfectants, and survive on surfaces for extended periods, posing a significant challenge in hospital environments (Harding et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harding et al., 2018.

claim: For Acinetobacter baylyi, resilience against external stresses was shown to be at least partly attributed to extracellular polysaccharides.
source: For Acinetobacter baylyi, a non-pathogenic species belonging to the same genus, resilience against external stresses was shown to be at least partly attributed to extracellular polysaccharides (Ophir and Gutnick, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ophir and Gutnick, 1994.

claim: Polysaccharides serve various protective roles against physical, chemical, and biological stresses.
source: These polysaccharides, whether secreted into the environment as biofilm matrix components (exopolysaccharides; EPS) or part of/attached to the bacterial membrane (like lipopolysaccharide, lipooligosaccharide, and capsule [capsular polysaccharide; CPS]), serve various protective roles against physical, chemical, and biological stresses (Flemming et al., 2023; Paczosa and Mecsas, 2016; Simpson and Trent, 2019; Whitfield et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Flemming et al., 2023; Paczosa and Mecsas, 2016; Simpson and Trent, 2019; Whitfield et al., 2020.

claim: In A. baumannii, the capsule is encoded within the genomic region between the fkpA and lldP genes known as the K locus.
source: In A. baumannii, the capsule, encoded within the genomic region between the fkpA and lldP genes known as the K locus (Wyres et al., 2020), is a key feature for many strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wyres et al., 2020.

claim: The K locus is usually arranged in three parts: genes encoding the CPS export machinery, a central region for capsule construction and processing, and a module for synthesizing simple sugar substrates.
source: The K locus is usually arranged in three parts: (1) the genes encoding the CPS export machinery (e.g., the wza, wzb, wzc operon); (2) a central region for capsule construction and processing (including the genes wzy and wzx, which encode the repeat unit polymerase and translocase, respectively); and (3) a module for synthesizing simple sugar substrates (Wyres et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wyres et al., 2020.

claim: The CPS assembles into complex, multibranched glycans that are tightly anchored to the outer membrane by the Wzi protein.
source: The CPS assembles into complex, multibranched glycans that are tightly anchored to the outer membrane by the Wzi protein, effectively encasing the cell in a protective polysaccharide shield (Tickner et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tickner et al., 2021.

claim: The capsule plays a crucial role in the virulence of A. baumannii, as demonstrated in in vivo studies using animal models where it provided resistance against complement-mediated killing.
source: This capsule plays a crucial role in the virulence of A. baumannii, as demonstrated in in vivo studies using animal models where it provided resistance against complement-mediated killing (Lees-Miller et al., 2013; Russo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lees-Miller et al., 2013 and Russo et al., 2010.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies targeting CPS have been shown to protect mice from infection by hypervirulent strains.
source: Furthermore, monoclonal antibodies targeting CPS have been shown to protect mice from infection by hypervirulent strains (Nielsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nielsen et al., 2017.

claim: Exposure to specific antibiotics at sub-MIC concentrations, such as chloramphenicol, can trigger the upregulation of K locus genes.
source: However, recent findings indicate that exposure to specific antibiotics at sub-MIC concentrations, such as of chloramphenicol, can trigger the upregulation of K locus genes (Geisinger and Isberg, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Geisinger and Isberg, 2015.

claim: The upregulation of K locus genes in response to chloramphenicol is mediated by the BfmRS two-component regulatory system, leading to enhanced virulence of A. baumannii.
source: This response is mediated by the BfmRS two-component regulatory system, leading to enhanced virulence of A. baumannii (Geisinger and Isberg, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Geisinger and Isberg, 2015.

claim: Extracellular polysaccharides such as EPS and CPS are known to protect against attacks by bacteria with a type VI secretion system (T6SS).
source: Extracellular polysaccharides such as EPS and CPS are known to protect against attacks by bacteria with a type VI secretion system (T6SS), a key player in bacterial warfare (Smith et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2023.

claim: The T6SS is found in 25% of Gram-negative bacteria and in more than 50% of β- and γ proteobacteria.
source: Found in 25% of Gram-negative bacteria and in more than 50% of β- and γ proteobacteria (Abby et al., 2016; Bingle et al., 2008), the T6SS is a contact-dependent contractile machinery that resembles inverted contractile bacteriophage tails (Basler et al., 2012; Leiman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Bingle et al., 2008.

claim: The T6SS is a contact-dependent contractile machinery that resembles inverted contractile bacteriophage tails.
source: Found in 25% of Gram-negative bacteria and in more than 50% of β- and γ proteobacteria (Abby et al., 2016; Bingle et al., 2008), the T6SS is a contact-dependent contractile machinery that resembles inverted contractile bacteriophage tails (Basler et al., 2012; Leiman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Basler et al., 2012 and Leiman et al., 2009.

claim: The T6SS features a membrane complex that extends across both the inner and outer bacterial membranes, with a baseplate-like structure connected within the cytoplasm.
source: The T6SS features a membrane complex that extends across both the inner and outer bacterial membranes, with a baseplate-like structure connected within the cytoplasm (Cherrak et al., 2018; Durand et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cherrak et al., 2018 and Durand et al., 2015.

claim: The baseplate of the T6SS is linked to an internal tube composed of Hcp hexamers, encased by a contractile sheath formed by TssB and TssC proteins.
source: The baseplate of the T6SS is linked to an internal tube composed of Hcp hexamers, encased by a contractile sheath formed by TssB and TssC proteins (Basler et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Basler et al., 2012.

claim: Upon contraction, the T6SS propels its inner tube, along with VgrG-PAAR spike proteins and toxins, into neighboring cells, leading to either growth arrest or cell death.
source: Upon contraction, the T6SS propels its inner tube, along with VgrG-PAAR spike proteins and toxins, into neighboring cells, leading to either growth arrest or cell death (Cherrak et al., 2019; Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cherrak et al., 2019 and Russell et al., 2014.

claim: Bacteria that possess the T6SS produce immunity proteins that specifically neutralize the bacterium's own toxic effector proteins, preventing self-intoxication or intoxication of kin.
source: To protect themselves from the effects of their own T6SS-launched toxins, bacteria that possess the T6SS also produce immunity proteins. These proteins specifically neutralize the bacterium's own toxic effector proteins, preventing self-intoxication or intoxication of kin (Hood et al., 2010; MacIntyre et al., 2010; Russell et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hood et al., 2010; MacIntyre et al., 2010; and Russell et al., 2011.

claim: Recent research has identified mechanisms of resistance to T6SS toxicity that do not involve immunity proteins, which include defenses provided by the production of EPS and capsules.
source: As mentioned above, recent research has identified mechanisms of resistance to T6SS toxicity that do not involve immunity proteins, which include defenses provided by the production of EPS (Granato et al., 2023; Hersch et al., 2020; Toska et al., 2018) and capsules (Flaugnatti et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Granato et al., 2023; Hersch et al., 2020; Toska et al., 2018; and Flaugnatti et al., 2021.

claim: The T6SS is widely found across Acinetobacter species, including A. baumannii.
source: The T6SS is widely found across Acinetobacter species, including A. baumannii (Dong et al., 2022; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2022 and Weber et al., 2013.

claim: The genes encoding the core components of the T6SS reside in a single locus in A. baumannii.
source: The genes encoding the core components of the T6SS reside in a single locus.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The vgrG genes in A. baumannii are scattered throughout the chromosome alongside effector/immunity modules.
source: However, the vgrG genes, which are crucial for the system's function, are scattered throughout the chromosome alongside effector/immunity modules (Eijkelkamp et al., 2014; Lewis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eijkelkamp et al., 2014 and Lewis et al., 2019.

claim: Some A. baumannii isolates express the T6SS under standard laboratory conditions, while others regulate expression via proteins such as H-NS.
source: The regulation of the T6SS in A. baumannii varies, with some isolates expressing the system under standard laboratory conditions, while others regulate expression via proteins such as H-NS (Eijkelkamp et al., 2013; Repizo et al., 2015; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eijkelkamp et al., 2013; Repizo et al., 2015; and Weber et al., 2013.

claim: TetR-like repressors encoded on large conjugative plasmids can suppress T6SS to aid conjugation and plasmid dissemination among cells.
source: Additionally, TetR-like repressors encoded on large conjugative plasmids, which also bear antibiotic resistance genes, can suppress T6SS to aid conjugation and plasmid dissemination among cells (Di Venanzio et al., 2019; Weber et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Di Venanzio et al., 2019 and Weber et al., 2015.

claim: The T6SS in A. baumannii significantly influences interbacterial dynamics, effectively targeting not only Gram-negative and -positive bacteria but also exhibiting antifungal capabilities.
source: Indeed, the T6SS in A. baumannii significantly influences interbacterial dynamics, effectively targeting not only Gram-negative and -positive bacteria (Le et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2013) but also exhibiting antifungal capabilities (Luo et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Le et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2013; and Luo et al., 2023.

claim: Studies in diverse animal models have shown that T6SS mutants do not incur a fitness cost.
source: However, although the T6SS confers competitive advantages to A. baumannii by targeting a wide range of microorganisms in vitro, studies in diverse animal models have shown that T6SS mutants do not incur a fitness cost (Weber et al., 2013), a finding that might be strain dependent, at least in the Galleria mellonella wax moth model of disease (Repizo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Weber et al., 2013 and Repizo et al., 2015.

claim: The CPS acts as a shield against T6SS attacks from rival bacteria.
source: Our findings reveal that the CPS acts as a shield against T6SS attacks from rival bacteria.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Under typical laboratory growth conditions, the presence of the surface-bound capsule reduces the efficacy of the bacterium's own T6SS.
source: However, we show that under typical laboratory growth conditions, the presence of the surface-bound capsule nonetheless reduces the efficacy of the bacterium's own T6SS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: T6SS impairment is further enhanced when CPS is overproduced due to genetic modifications or antibiotic treatment.
source: This T6SS impairment is further enhanced when CPS is overproduced due to genetic modifications or antibiotic treatment.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The bacterium adjusts the level of the T6SS inner tube protein Hcp according to its secretion capacity, by initiating a degradation process involving the ClpXP protease.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the bacterium adjusts the level of the T6SS inner tube protein Hcp according to its secretion capacity, by initiating a degradation process involving the ClpXP protease.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: A. baumannii A118 possesses the K locus, located between the fkpA and lldP genes.
source: The A118 strain was found to possess the K locus, located between the fkpA and lldP genes (Vesel and Blokesch, 2021), suggesting its encapsulated nature.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vesel and Blokesch, 2021.

claim: Deleting the itrA gene in A. baumannii A118 results in a three-log decrease in survival compared to the WT strain when challenged with rabbit serum.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, deleting the itrA gene resulted in a three-log decrease in survival compared to both the WT strain and the mock control conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Complement-dependent killing of the non-capsulated strain was not observed when the serum was heat-inactivated before being added to the bacteria.
source: This complement-dependent killing of the non-capsulated strain was not observed when the serum was heat-inactivated before being added to the bacteria (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ItrA plays a critical role in CPS synthesis in A. baumannii A118.
source: Collectively, and in accordance with current literature (Kenyon and Hall, 2013; Lees-Miller et al., 2013), our findings establish the critical role of ItrA in CPS synthesis, and confirm that A. baumannii A118 possesses a capsule.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and citations to Kenyon and Hall, 2013 and Lees-Miller et al., 2013.

claim: The lack of CPS in the A. baumannii prey (ΔitrA) resulted in increased susceptibility to T6SS-mediated attacks by E. cloacae.
source: Conversely, the lack of CPS in the A. baumannii prey (ΔitrA-Tn) resulted in increased susceptibility to T6SS-mediated attacks by E. cloacae (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The non-capsulated strain (ΔitrA) exhibited full resistance to E. cloacae's T6SS attacks when A. baumannii's T6SS is functional.
source: When we conducted the experiment again under conditions that allow A. baumannii's T6SS to function (T6SS+), we observed an unexpected outcome: the non-capsulated strain (ΔitrA) exhibited full resistance to E. cloacae's T6SS attacks, mirroring the resistance shown by the capsulated WT strain (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A. baumannii A118 possesses an active antibacterial T6SS when tested under standard laboratory conditions.
source: These results verify that A. baumannii A118 indeed possesses an active antibacterial T6SS when tested under standard laboratory conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CPS-deficient A. baumannii (ΔitrA) exhibits increased T6SS-mediated killing activity compared to the WT strain at a 1:5 attacker:prey ratio.
source: Under these conditions, we noted decreased T6SS-mediated killing activity in the WT strain compared to the ΔitrA strain, while no difference was noted between the WT and ΔpglL strains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: T6SS-mediated killing activity is elevated in the absence of CPS.
source: This suggests that T6SS-mediated killing activity is elevated in the absence of CPS and that the O-glycosylation pathway does not contribute to this phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The amount of Hcp detected in the supernatant was considerably higher in the ΔitrA strain compared to the WT or the ΔpglL mutant.
source: Importantly, while all strains produced Hcp at comparable levels, the amount of Hcp detected in the supernatant was considerably higher in the ΔitrA strain compared to the WT or the ΔpglL mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: T6SS secretion activity is enhanced in the absence of the CPS.
source: This finding reinforces the notion that T6SS secretion activity is enhanced in the absence of the CPS.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hcp secretion data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The capsule's presence or absence does not affect the production or assembly of the T6SS in A. baumannii A118.
source: This data indicates that the capsule's presence or absence does not affect the production or assembly of the T6SS in A. baumannii A118.
evidence: This is inferred from the T6SS assembly data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: The enhanced T6SS activity in the non-capsulated mutant (ΔitrA) is likely due to an increase in the number of successful T6SS firing events.
source: This suggests that the capsule may serve as an additional barrier the T6SS has to traverse to be expelled from the cell. Supporting this theory, our analysis reveals that the enhanced T6SS activity in the non-capsulated mutant (ΔitrA) is not due to a higher number of T6SS assemblies but likely due to an increase in the number of successful T6SS firing events.
evidence: This is inferred from the T6SS assembly and secretion data.

claim: In Campylobacter jejuni, the T6SS was only cytotoxic to red blood cells in a capsule-deficient context.
source: This finding is in line with previous reports on Campylobacter jejuni, where the T6SS was only cytotoxic to red blood cells in a capsule-deficient context (Bleumink-Pluym et al., 2013), leading to the hypothesis that the capsule acts as a physical barrier, limiting T6SS's ability to directly interact with target cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bleumink-Pluym et al., 2013.

claim: A substitution in the Walker A motif of the Wzc protein induces a mucoviscous phenotype characterized by abnormally high molecular weight polysaccharides predominantly found in the supernatant and only loosely attached to the cell.
source: Indeed, Geisinger and Isberg demonstrated that a substitution in the Walker A motif of the Wzc protein, which controls the size of exported polysaccharides, induces in a mucoviscous phenotype characterized by abnormally high molecular weight polysaccharides predominantly found in the supernatant and only loosely attached to the cell.
evidence: This claim is based on prior work by Geisinger and Isberg, 2015.

claim: Removing bfmS disrupts the phosphorylation cascade, resulting in the overproduction of the K locus gene cluster.
source: The BfmS histidine kinase within this system typically represses K locus expression by phosphorylation of the response regulator BfmR (Palethorpe et al., 2022). Consequently, removing bfmS disrupts this phosphorylation cascade, resulting in the overproduction of the K locus gene cluster (Geisinger and Isberg, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Palethorpe et al., 2022 and Geisinger and Isberg, 2015.

claim: The ΔbfmS mutant showed increased resistance to serum-mediated killing.
source: The ΔbfmS mutant showed increased resistance to serum-mediated killing (Figure 3A), aligned with an augmented presence of cell-associated CPS material (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The Wzc[K547Q] mutant displayed heightened susceptibility to the rabbit serum.
source: Conversely, the Wzc[K547Q] mutant displayed heightened susceptibility to the rabbit serum (Figure 3A), which correlates with the faint CPS signal detected in the cell fraction by Alcian blue staining (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Dysregulation in polysaccharide chain length can adversely affect the capsule's protective properties.
source: This indicates that dysregulation in polysaccharide chain length can adversely affect the capsule's protective properties.
evidence: This is inferred from the serum killing and CPS staining data for the Wzc[K547Q] mutant.

claim: The ΔbfmS mutant exhibits a significant reduction in its ability to kill E. coli prey cells.
source: The results reveal that the ΔbfmS mutant exhibits a significant reduction in its ability to kill E. coli prey cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The double mutant ΔbfmSΔitrA reinstated the strain's killing ability.
source: To rule out the possibility of the bfmS mutation having broad effects on T6SS production or function, we also evaluated the double mutant ΔbfmSΔitrA, which reinstated the strain's killing ability (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The mutant lacking bfmS showed a significant impairment in its Hcp secretion activity.
source: Specifically, the mutant lacking bfmS showed a significant impairment in its Hcp secretion activity, whereas the ΔbfmSΔitrA double mutant reflected the secretion pattern of the ΔitrA strain (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The deletion of bfmS in environmental A. baumannii isolates (29D2 and 86II/2C) resulted in the impairment of the T6SS-mediated killing.
source: Importantly, the deletion of bfmS in these strains also resulted in the impairment of the T6SS-mediated killing. These findings indicate that bfmS affects T6SS-mediated killing activity across different strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The Wzc[K547Q] variant demonstrated T6SS-mediated killing similar to that observed in the WT.
source: Unlike the ΔbfmS phenotypes, the Wzc[K547Q] variant demonstrated T6SS-mediated killing similar to that observed in the WT, as shown in Figure 3C.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The WT cells were surrounded by material forming large finger-like projections extending about 150 nm from the cell surface, arranged in a semi-regular pattern of projections and spaces.
source: The WT cells were surrounded by material forming large finger-like projections extending about 150 nm from the cell surface, arranged in a semi-regular pattern of projections and spaces.
evidence: This claim is based on TEM observations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Wzc[K547Q] variant lacked finger-like CPS structures, appearing similar to the ΔitrA mutant.
source: Notably, the Wzc[K547Q] variant also lacked these structures, appearing similar to the ΔitrA mutant.
evidence: This claim is based on TEM observations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The bfmS mutant exhibited a dense, tangled, mesh-like network of CPS covering the cell surface, similar to the WT but without the clear periodic spaces.
source: In contrast, the bfmS mutant exhibited a dense, tangled, mesh-like network of CPS covering the cell surface, similar to the WT but without the clear periodic spaces.
evidence: This claim is based on TEM observations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Disruption in the organized, finger-like structure of the capsule, as seen with overexpression of the K-locus, leads to a suppression of T6SS-mediated killing activity and blocks Hcp secretion.
source: Taken all together, these results indicate that disruption in the organized, finger-like structure of the capsule, as seen with overexpression of the K-locus, leads to a suppression of T6SS-mediated killing activity and blocks Hcp secretion.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined TEM, killing, and secretion data.

claim: A. baumannii isolate 17978 boosts CPS production via the BfmRS two component system in response to sub-minimal inhibitory concentrations (sub-MIC) of chloramphenicol.
source: It has been shown that the A. baumannii isolate 17978 boosts CPS production via the BfmRS two component system in response to sub-minimal inhibitory concentrations (sub-MIC) of chloramphenicol (Geisinger and Isberg, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Geisinger and Isberg, 2015.

claim: When A. baumannii A118 was exposed to various chloramphenicol concentrations, the capsule induction by the antibiotic was dose-dependent.
source: When we exposed A. baumannii A118 to various chloramphenicol concentrations, we found that the capsule induction by the antibiotic was dose-dependent, as evidenced by increased CPS presence in the supernatant (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Chloramphenicol-induced capsule production disrupts T6SS-mediated killing activity.
source: This suggests that chloramphenicol-induced capsule production disrupts T6SS-mediated killing activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the killing assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The inhibition of T6SS by increased capsule production, as observed with the ΔbfmS mutant, could be relevant in natural conditions that A. baumannii might encounter, such as the presence of sub-MIC antibiotics in the environment.
source: Collectively, this data suggests that the inhibition of T6SS by increased capsule production, as observed with the ΔbfmS mutant, could be relevant in natural conditions that A. baumannii might encounter, such as the presence of sub-MIC antibiotics in the environment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The antibiotic-induced enhancement of capsule production represents a non-mutational phenotype, which can be reversed upon removal of the antibiotic.
source: Interestingly, Geisinger and Isberg demonstrated that the antibiotic-induced enhancement of capsule production represents a non-mutational phenotype, which can be reversed upon removal of the antibiotic (Geisinger and Isberg, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Geisinger and Isberg, 2015.

claim: A recent investigation into A. baylyi revealed the presence of TslA, a periplasmic protein essential for precise assembly of the T6SS machinery at points of contact with other cells.
source: A recent investigation into A. baylyi revealed the presence of TslA, a periplasmic protein essential for precise assembly of the T6SS machinery at points of contact with other cells, aiming to prevent wasteful T6SS firing events (Lin et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2022.

claim: AsaA, the TslA homolog in A. baumannii, has been shown to play a role in efficient T6SS activity.
source: Importantly, the periplasmic Acinetobacter type six secretion system-associated A protein (AsaA), which is the TslA homolog in A. baumannii, has been shown to play a role in efficient T6SS activity (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: AsaA/TslA impacts the assembly or stability of the T6SS through its interaction with the membrane complex protein TssM.
source: Indeed, Li et al. suggested that AsaA/TslA impacts the assembly or stability of the T6SS through its interaction with the membrane complex protein TssM (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: There was a significant 5.6-fold decrease in T6SS assembly in the ΔtslA mutant (17.6 ± 8.7%) compared to the WT (99.0 ± 1.4%).
source: We noted a significant 5.6-fold decrease in T6SS assembly in the ΔtslA mutant (17.6 ± 8.7%) compared to the WT (99.0 ± 1.4%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ΔbfmS mutant exhibited a more moderate 1.9-fold reduction in T6SS assembly (50.8 ± 8.8%) in comparison to the WT.
source: Meanwhile, the ΔbfmS mutant exhibited a more moderate 1.9-fold reduction (50.8 ± 8.8%) in comparison to the WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ΔbfmSΔitrA double mutant showed T6SS assembly rates (97.6 ± 1.0%) similar to both the WT and ΔitrA (99.2 ± 1.0%) strains.
source: Remarkably, the ΔbfmSΔitrA double mutant showed T6SS assembly rates (97.6 ± 1.0%) similar to both the WT and ΔitrA (99.2 ± 1.0%) strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The capsule's overproduction in ΔbfmS only partially influences T6SS assembly.
source: These findings suggest that the capsule's overproduction in ΔbfmS only partially influences T6SS assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the T6SS assembly data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The removal of tslA led to a decrease in T6SS-mediated killing and the amount of secreted Hcp.
source: In line with results obtained previously in A. baylyi (Ringel et al., 2017) and A. baumannii ATCC17978 (Kandolo et al., 2023; Li et al., 2019), the removal of tslA led to a decrease in T6SS-mediated killing and the amount of secreted Hcp.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D, and citations to Ringel et al., 2017; Kandolo et al., 2023; and Li et al., 2019.

claim: The tslA mutant displayed significantly higher levels of killing and Hcp secretion compared to the ΔbfmS mutant under identical experimental conditions.
source: Interestingly, the tslA mutant displayed significantly higher levels of killing (Figure 5C) and Hcp secretion (Figure 5D) compared to the ΔbfmS mutant under identical experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The diminished killing and secretion performance seen in the ΔbfmS mutant cannot be solely attributed to a defect in cell–cell contact sensing and T6SS assembly.
source: Taken together, these findings collectively indicate that the diminished killing and secretion performance seen in the ΔbfmS mutant cannot be solely attributed to a defect in cell–cell contact sensing and T6SS assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined assembly, killing, and secretion data.

claim: In stationary phase cultures, Hcp was undetectable in the ΔbfmS mutant but present at WT levels in the ΔbfmSΔitrA double mutant.
source: Our observations revealed that, in stationary phase cultures, Hcp was undetectable in the ΔbfmS mutant but present at WT levels in the ΔbfmSΔitrA double mutant (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Deletion of tssB led to the disappearance of Hcp in stationary phase.
source: Surprisingly, similar to the ΔbfmS mutant, deletion of tssB led to the disappearance of Hcp in stationary phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Hcp downregulation upon blocking secretion might be a common feature in A. baumannii.
source: Comparable results were obtained with secretion-impaired mutants of A. baumannii strains 29D2 and 86II/2C (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Hcp downregulation upon blocking secretion might be a common feature in A. baumannii.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The decrease in Hcp protein levels in ΔtssB occurred between 6 and 11 hr of growth.
source: Notably, the decrease in Hcp protein levels in ΔtssB occurred between 6 and 11 hr of growth (Figure 6C), coinciding with the transition to late stationary phase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There were no statistically significant changes in hcp transcript levels between the WT and the ΔtssB mutant throughout the experiment.
source: However, there were no statistically significant changes in hcp transcript levels between the WT and the ΔtssB mutant throughout the experiment (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The effects of secretion impairment and Hcp intracellular accumulation may be regulated post-transcriptionally.
source: These results suggest that the effects of secretion impairment and Hcp intracellular accumulation may be regulated post-transcriptionally.
evidence: This is inferred from the protein and transcript level data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: In the Δhcp background containing the hcp-carrying plasmid, Hcp protein production remained largely undetectable despite high transcript levels.
source: In contrast, in the Δhcp background containing the hcp-carrying plasmid (Δhcp + p-hcp), we observed similarly high transcript levels as for the WT condition (WT + p-hcp) (Figure 7A), yet Hcp protein production remained largely undetectable (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The Δhcp mutant may exhibit a polar effect that leads to Hcp accumulation upon complementation in trans.
source: This observation suggests that, despite careful genetic engineering, the Δhcp mutant may exhibit a polar effect that leads to Hcp accumulation upon complementation in trans, thereby mimicking the secretion-impaired ∆tssB mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementation data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Deletion of clpXP resulted in intracellular Hcp accumulation over time in both the WT and tssB-deficient backgrounds.
source: In contrast, deletion of clpXP resulted in intracellular Hcp accumulation over time in both the WT and tssB-deficient backgrounds, indicating that ClpXP may be involved in the degradation mechanism of Hcp when secretion is impaired in the otherwise WT background (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Hcp levels were comparable to WT in the ΔtssBΔclpXP and ΔbfmSΔclpXP double mutants.
source: Supporting this idea is the observation that, although undetectable when secretion is blocked in the ∆tssB and ΔbfmS strains, Hcp levels were comparable to WT in the ΔtssBΔclpXP and ΔbfmSΔclpXP double mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There were no statistically significant differences in the expression levels of clpX and clpP between the WT and the ΔtssB background at any of the tested time points.
source: However, there were no statistically significant differences in the expression levels of clpX and clpP between the WT and the ΔtssB background at any of the tested time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The crystal structure of the Hcp protein from A. baumannii strain AB0057 shows that its C-terminal domain is exposed when represented as a hexamer.
source: Interestingly, when represented as a hexamer, the crystal structure of the Hcp protein from A. baumannii strain AB0057 (Ruiz et al., 2015) shows that its C-terminal domain is exposed, potentially making it accessible for interaction with ClpX and subsequent degradation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on structural data from Ruiz et al., 2015, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In the Δhcp background of A. baumannii, high protein levels of Hcp variants lacking the last 11 amino acids or with Ala-to-Asp substitutions in the last two amino acids were detected, whereas native Hcp was heavily degraded.
source: Importantly, in the Δhcp background of A. baumannii, we also detected high protein levels of these two modified Hcp versions (p-hcpCTDΔ11 and p-hcp[A166D/A167D]), whereas native Hcp was again heavily degraded (p-hcp) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The Hcp C-terminus plays a crucial role for its degradation by the ClpXP machinery.
source: These results suggest that the Hcp C-terminus plays a crucial for its degradation by the ClpXP machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the C-terminal variant data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A. baumannii has evolved a sophisticated regulation of its T6SS, closely tied to the strain's secretion capacity to prevent unnecessary protein accumulation.
source: More broadly, these observations indicate that A. baumannii has evolved a sophisticated regulation of its T6SS, closely tied to the strain's secretion capacity to prevent unnecessary protein accumulation.
evidence: This is a general conclusion inferred from the Hcp degradation data.

claim: Both the capsule and the T6SS independently offer protection during antagonistic interactions with competitors.
source: Notably, we demonstrated that both the capsule and the T6SS independently offer protection during antagonistic interactions with competitors, and these protective effects might be synergistic, at least under laboratory conditions (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Overproduction of the capsule in A. baumannii A118 impedes T6SS activity by hindering its assembly, potentially due to increased membrane tension from excess polysaccharides affecting membrane complex anchoring.
source: However, overproduction of the capsule in A. baumannii A118 impedes T6SS activity by hindering its assembly, potentially due to increased membrane tension from excess polysaccharides affecting membrane complex anchoring (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Capsule overproduction disrupts the organization of polysaccharides on the cell surface, likely impairing proper T6SS secretion.
source: Furthermore, capsule overproduction disrupts the organization of polysaccharides on the cell surface, likely impairing proper T6SS secretion (Figure 8).
evidence: This is inferred from the TEM and secretion data.

claim: The inhibition of T6SS activity observed in the capsule-overexpressing mutant (ΔbfmS) also occurs under conditions of antibiotic-induced capsule overexpression.
source: Interestingly, the inhibition of T6SS activity that we observed in the capsule-overexpressing mutant (ΔbfmS) also occurs under conditions of antibiotic-induced capsule overexpression.
evidence: This is based on the chloramphenicol treatment data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The inhibition of T6SS by capsule overproduction is an adaptive response to withstand antibiotic exposure.
source: It is plausible that this inhibition is an adaptive response to withstand antibiotic exposure.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: In secretion-impaired strains, the accumulation of Hcp is mitigated by a degradation mechanism involving the general ClpXP protease machinery.
source: Furthermore, we found that in secretion-impaired strains, the accumulation of Hcp is mitigated by a degradation mechanism involving the general ClpXP protease machinery (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Hcp degradation may serve as a strategy to alleviate proteotoxic stress and conserve energy, especially under unfavorable conditions such as antibiotic exposure.
source: Given that the production of the T6SS involves the continuous synthesis and secretion of hundreds of protein components, we speculate that this degradation may serve as a strategy to alleviate proteotoxic stress and conserve energy, especially under unfavorable conditions such as antibiotic exposure.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the Hcp degradation findings.
